---
title: "Computational model of aesthetics"
description: "Attention, perceptual compression, and learning progress as aesthetic reward."
toc-depth: 3
---

## Overview

This model proposes that beauty helps guide attention toward experiences from
which an organism can learn. As its model of perceptual representations
improves, a sense of beauty acts as an internal reward that encourages
attention. Perception encodes sensory information under limited processing
capacity; learning the distribution of these representations can reduce the cost
of coding them.

**First-version scope:** the encoder and latent probability model have no
explicit temporal-history input. Learning still accumulates past experience in
their parameters. More realistic future models may incorporate temporal
conditioning.

**Model status:** conceptual hypothesis. The mathematical information bound is
distinct from the proposed biological interpretation and aesthetic mechanism.

## Model components

  | Component               | Role                                                                 |
  | ---                     | ---                                                                  |
  | Attention policy $\pi$  | Selects stimuli given the agent’s conditioning state $s$.            |
  | Perceptual channel $F$  | Maps raw sensory input $X$ to a latent representation $Z$.           |
  | Latent model $R_\theta$ | Assigns a normalized probability distribution to perceptual latents. |
  | Aesthetic reward        | Heuristically tracks learning progress and reinforces attention.     |

**Information flow:** sensory input → $F$ → latent representation → likelihood
under $R_\theta$ → estimated learning progress → reward for attention.

### Attention

Attention is a learned reinforcement-learning policy:

$$
  \pi(x \mid s) = P(\text{attend to stimulus }x \mid \text{state }s).
$$

Here $x$ is a stimulus and $s$ summarizes the conditions under which attention
is selected. The policy learns to favor choices that yield aesthetic reward.
Retaining this policy state does not require temporal conditioning of $F$ or
$R$.

### Perceptual representation

A perceptual encoder turns sensory input into an internal representation, called
a latent. Rate--distortion theory describes the trade-off between information
retained and errors introduced by compression [@sims2016]:

$$
  F(z \mid x) = P(Z = z \mid X = x).
$$

Biological code complexity is assumed to be capacity-limited and costly.
Information rate is our proposed surrogate for that cost. Useful information
must be retained through a task-performance or distortion requirement;
minimizing complexity alone admits an uninformative channel.

### Latent probability model

The learned model $R_\theta(z)$, also called the latent prior, describes which
representations are likely. It can capture structure within a representation
without predicting the next time step from previous latents or actions. Its
parameters $\theta$ reflect learning experience, but history is not an explicit
input.

$R_\theta$ must be a normalized probability mass function or density, not an
arbitrary scalar score. Latent surprise is:

$$
  \ell_\theta(z) = -\log R_\theta(z).
$$

This first version implements latent density learning. Interpreting it as a
component of a biological world model remains a hypothesis.

## Information cost and capacity

### Measuring information

Mutual information measures how much the latent representation tells us about
sensory input. Expected KL divergence---a measure of difference between
distributions---provides an upper bound on this information rate.

Under the joint distribution $p(x)F(z \mid x)$, the aggregate latent
distribution is:

$$
  q_F(z) = \int p(x)F(z \mid x)\,dx.
$$

The variational rate identity underlying @alemi2018 gives:

$$
  \mathcal C(F,\theta)
  = \mathbb E_X D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(F(\cdot \mid X)\Vert R_\theta\big)
$$

$$
  \mathcal C(F,\theta) = I_F(X;Z) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_F\Vert R_\theta\big)
                       \ge I_F(X;Z).
$$

**Interpretation:** expected KL equals information rate plus prior mismatch. For
fixed $F$ and $p(x)$, an unrestricted optimal prior matches $q_F$ and makes the
bound tight. A restricted learned prior may leave a positive gap.

Learning $R$ reduces prior mismatch, not the information retained by a fixed
encoder under a fixed input distribution. Improved coding efficiency is the
proposed biological interpretation; actual savings require a mechanism that
exploits the learned distribution. The bound alone does not establish such a
mechanism in organisms.

### Capacity constraint and complexity penalty

**Visual example:** [Rate--distortion and prior
mismatch](rate-distortion-prior.qmd) shows how learning the prior closes a KL
gap above a rate--distortion curve while holding the encoder fixed.

The information rate is bounded by capacity $K$:

$$
  I_F(X;Z) \le K.
$$

Imposing $\mathcal C(F,\theta) \le K$ is sufficient but may be conservative when
the prior is mismatched. Complexity can also enter the organism's objective as a
penalty. A candidate VAE objective with reconstruction log-loss is specified
below. Its penalty weight, likelihood family, and relationship to capacity and
behavioral usefulness remain open.

**Technical conditions:** finite KL requires appropriate prior support and a
well-defined rate; base-2 logs yield bits and natural logs yield nats. For
continuous representations, deterministic encoders may require noise or
quantization to obtain a finite information rate.

## Learning and aesthetic reward

### Learning informative representations

Representations must preserve meaningful differences between inputs. If every
input produced the same representation, prediction would be easy but perception
would convey no useful information.

Latent predictive learning offers one possible mechanism for acquiring $F$
before the simplified model's learning phase [@halvagal2023]:

- Predictive plasticity brings representations of temporally adjacent inputs
  together, supporting invariance.
- Hebbian plasticity preserves activity variation and prevents representational
  collapse.
- Prediction occurs in latent space without requiring sensory reconstruction.

That temporal training mechanism is distinct from the history-free density model
used here. Connecting it to our probabilistic prior and aesthetic reward is our
synthesis, not a result established by that paper. Preventing collapse does not
itself specify which information is task-relevant.

### Initial option: freeze an already-useful encoder

Assume $F$ learned useful representations on an earlier task. Freeze its
parameters (a stop-gradient equivalent) and train only $R_\theta$. This prevents
encoder collapse during this phase: the prior cannot improve by making $F$
discard distinctions.

For a fixed input distribution, prior learning reduces mismatch in $\mathcal C$
while $I_F(X;Z)$ remains fixed. Changing which stimuli are attended can change
the input distribution, so comparisons of learning progress must distinguish
model improvement from stimulus-selection effects. Learning the initial useful
$F$ remains a separate problem.

### Initial option: learn representations with a VAE

A variational autoencoder is a candidate starting point for jointly learning
representations and their prior. Add a decoder $p_\psi(x \mid z)$ that
reconstructs sensory input from the latent. On attended stimuli, use
reconstruction log-loss, following @alemi2018 [Eqs. 2--6]:

$$
  \mathcal D(F,\psi)
  = \mathbb E_{X \sim p_{\mathrm{att}},\,Z \sim F( \cdot \mid X)}[-\log p_\psi(X \mid Z)].
$$

The candidate joint objective is:

$$
  \min_{F,\theta,\psi}\;\mathcal D(F,\psi) + \beta\mathcal C(F,\theta),
  \qquad
  \beta \geq 0.
$$

$\mathcal C$ is the expected encoder/prior KL defined above, evaluated on the
same attended-input distribution. At $\beta = 1$ this is the negative ELBO;
other weights adjust the reconstruction--compression trade-off.

**Why it helps:** reconstruction encourages $F$ to retain information needed to
explain the input, while the prior learns its latent distribution. Under
well-defined entropy and log-loss, the corresponding bound is:

$$
  H(X) - \mathcal D \leq I_F(X;Z).
$$

Beating the optimal input-independent reconstruction log-loss baseline therefore
requires informative latents. The likelihood family determines which errors
matter; a fixed-variance isotropic Gaussian gives squared-error loss up to
scaling and a constant.

**Scope:** this is a candidate for useful representations, not a guarantee
against collapse or of behavioral usefulness. An expressive decoder can ignore
$Z$; @alemi2018 show that good ELBO alone does not ensure useful latents.
Outcomes depend on likelihood, architecture, compression weight, and stimulus
coverage. Assess rate and distortion separately: positive expected KL alone does
not establish informative latents because it includes prior mismatch.

### Learning progress as reward

Let $E(t)$ denote latent prediction error in the continually learned model:

$$
  \mathrm{LP}(t) = -\frac{dE(t)}{dt}.
$$

A natural error metric for this version is expected negative log likelihood
under $R_\theta$. With $F$ and the evaluation distribution held fixed, a
discrete estimate of improvement is:

$$
  \mathrm{LP}
  = \mathbb E_{Z \sim q_{\mathrm{eval}}}\big[\log R_{\theta_{\mathrm{after}}}(Z) - \log R_{\theta_{\mathrm{before}}}(Z)\big].
$$

This is improvement over an update interval; dividing by its duration gives a
rate. Aesthetic reward is hypothesized to track this improvement, rather than
simply high likelihood or familiarity. The exact estimator and mapping to reward
remain open. Held-out examples can help distinguish generalizable learning from
memorization of just-trained items.

The aesthetic account is intended to extend @schmidhuber2009 and @brielmann2022.
The precise extensions and literature comparison remain to be established
against the source papers.

### Candidate reward: selecting efficient learning samples

One candidate aesthetic reward favors attention policies that sample latents
efficiently for learning the prior. The established result concerns the variance
of a gradient estimate; interpreting this efficiency as a proxy for learning
progress remains a model hypothesis. For this derivation, freeze the encoder $F$
and the reference stimulus distribution $p(x)$. Write their aggregate posterior
as $p(z) = q_F(z)$, using the definition above. This target distribution is
fixed, not necessarily uniform. Attention instead produces the state-conditional
latent distribution
$$
  q_\pi(z \mid s) = \int \pi(x \mid s)F(z \mid x)\,dx.
$$
Suppose the prior learns by stochastic gradient descent on expected negative log
likelihood. Define the loss and its per-latent gradient as
$$
  L(\theta) = \mathbb E_{p(Z)}[-\log R_\theta(Z)],
  \qquad
  g_\theta(z) = \nabla_\theta[-\log R_\theta(z)].
$$
Sampling $X \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s)$ and then $Z \sim F(\cdot \mid X)$ gives a
sample from $q_\pi(\cdot \mid s)$. To estimate the gradient for the fixed target
$p$, rather than for the attended distribution, weight that sample by the
**importance ratio**:
$$
  \widehat g(Z,s) = \frac{p(Z)}{q_\pi(Z \mid s)}g_\theta(Z).
$$
This corrects for how attention changes sampling frequency, so that
$\mathbb E[\widehat g \mid s] = \nabla_\theta L$. Without this correction,
attention generally changes the expected update as well as its variance.
@alain2016 [Theorem 1] show that the proposal minimizing the trace of the
estimator's covariance---the sum of the variances of its gradient
components---is
$$
  q_\theta^*(z) = \frac{p(z)\|g_\theta(z)\|_2}{C_\theta},
  \qquad
  C_\theta = \mathbb E_{p(Z)}\|g_\theta(Z)\|_2.
$$
Assume $0 < C_\theta < \infty$, appropriate sampling support wherever
$p(z)g_\theta(z)$ is nonzero, and finite estimator second moments for the
proposals being compared. Hold $\theta$ fixed during each policy comparison.
This motivates the following KL objective for attention:
$$
  J_s(\pi;\theta)
  = \mathbb E_{q_\pi(Z \mid s)} [\log p(Z) + \log\|g_\theta(Z)\|_2]
    + H_{q_\pi}(Z \mid s)
$$
$$
  J_s(\pi;\theta)
  = \log C_\theta
    - D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_\pi(\cdot \mid s)\Vert q_\theta^*\big).
$$
Here $H_{q_\pi}(Z \mid s) = -\mathbb E_{q_\pi}\log q_\pi(Z \mid s)$ is the
entropy of the induced latent distribution at state $s$ (differential entropy
for continuous latents). Assume these terms are well-defined. Because KL
divergence is nonnegative and vanishes when its distributions match, **the
global maximum over unrestricted latent sampling distributions occurs at the
variance-optimal proposal $q_\theta^*$**. An attention policy attains this
maximum only if its mixtures of $F(z \mid x)$ can realize that proposal. The
unknown $\log p(z)$ could be approximated by $\log R_\theta(z)$ in the reward.
This yields the candidate sample reward
$$
  a_\theta(z,s;\pi) = \log R_\theta(z) + \log\|g_\theta(z)\|_2
                      - \log q_\pi(z \mid s).
$$
Its expected value has the same form as $J_s$, but its unrestricted optimum is
proportional to $R_\theta(z)\|g_\theta(z)\|_2$. It approximates the
variance-optimal proposal to the extent that this substitution approximates the
true target. The exact global-optimum statement above uses $p(z)$. Neither
statement establishes that reward magnitude measures actual learning progress or
that every improvement in the KL objective reduces variance.

**Status:** the shared global optimum is a mathematical result. Treating this
objective as an estimate of learning progress remains a hypothesis. It does not
establish a monotonic relationship between KL divergence and gradient variance,
or measure the actual reduction in prior mismatch over an update interval.

## Future extension: temporal conditioning

More realistic models may let both perception and the latent prior depend on
shared temporal context:

$$
  F(z_t \mid x_t,h_t),\qquad R_\theta(z_t \mid h_t),
  \qquad
  H_t = (Z_{t-1},A_{t-1})\ \text{as one candidate}.
$$

The information-rate formulation would then use $I_F(X;Z \mid H)$, with a
corresponding conditional prior-mismatch term. This could capture sequence
expectations and order effects, including those important in music. It is not
required for the first version; context choice and its availability to encoding
and decoding processes would need to be specified.

@lai2025 provide behavioral evidence for conditional policy compression,
measuring state-to-action information $I(S_t;A_t \mid S_{t-1})$. Applying that
principle to a perceptual channel is a proposed extension, not direct evidence
for a perceptual capacity bound. A separate attention-policy complexity penalty
is not currently part of the model.

## Open questions

- **Useful representation:** should initial experiments freeze a previously
  useful encoder or jointly learn it with the candidate VAE objective? Which
  likelihood, architecture, and rate--distortion trade-off preserve useful
  information?
- **Objective:** how should capacity, complexity cost, and reward be combined
  and weighted?
- **Latent model:** which normalized density family captures the regularities
  people learn?
- **Aesthetic signal:** how is progress estimated and mapped to reward, and what
  is the RL time horizon? How can it be separated from familiarity,
  memorization, changing latent targets, or shifts toward easier stimuli?
- **Attention--perception interface:** how does policy state $s$ govern stimulus
  sampling and the distribution encountered by $F$ and $R$?
- **Importance ratio:** how can the organism tractably estimate
  $p(z)/q_\pi(z \mid s)$ for prior updates, given an unknown aggregate posterior
  and an attention-induced latent mixture? Approximating $p$ by $R_\theta$ in
  the selection reward does not supply an unbiased importance ratio for learning
  $p$.
- **Conditional entropy:** how can the organism tractably estimate
  $H_{q_\pi}(Z \mid s)$, or the sample term $-\log q_\pi(z \mid s)$? This is
  entropy of the latent mixture induced by attention, not simply entropy of the
  attention policy or of $F(Z \mid X)$.
- **KL and gradient variance:** sharing a global optimum does not guarantee that
  gradient-estimator variance increases monotonically with
  $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\pi\Vert q_\theta^*)$. Under what additional conditions
  does reducing this KL reduce variance and improve learning? Restrictions on
  attainable latent distributions can also make the KL-optimal and
  variance-optimal policies differ.
- **Temporal extension:** when is explicit context necessary, and what history
  should it contain?

## Evidence and source coverage

The biological coding-cost interpretation, learned-prior mechanism, and
aesthetic synthesis are model hypotheses. Empirical findings and mathematical
identities support components without establishing the complete account.

The account brings together theories of perceptual compression, representation
learning, and intrinsic reward. Further literature analysis is needed to
establish its precise relationship to existing theories of aesthetics and to
assess the biological interpretation of its information cost.

**Topics:** computational aesthetics; attention; reinforcement learning;
intrinsic reward; learning progress; rate--distortion; perceptual
representation; mutual information; latent density learning.
